purpose: Cefiderocol is a powerful antibiotic used to treat serious bacterial infections, especially those caused by hard-to-treat bacteria that are resistant to many other antibiotics. It is typically used for infections in the urinary tract, lungs, or bloodstream. Doctors usually prescribe it when other antibiotics have not worked or are not expected to work.
how_it_works: This antibiotic uses a clever trick to get inside bacteria — it disguises itself as iron, which bacteria need to survive. The bacteria actually pull the drug inside themselves thinking it is iron, like a Trojan horse. Once inside, cefiderocol damages the bacterial cell wall, causing the bacteria to break apart and die.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include diarrhea, nausea, vomiting, constipation, rash, and elevated liver enzyme levels in your blood tests. You may also experience headache, low potassium levels, or swelling. Some patients develop a new infection with a different organism, including a fungal infection, during or after treatment.
warnings: This medication can cause serious allergic reactions, especially if you have had a prior reaction to penicillin or other cephalosporin antibiotics — tell your doctor right away if you develop hives, difficulty breathing, or swelling. It may also cause severe diarrhea due to a bacterial infection called C. difficile, which can happen even weeks after finishing treatment. Use with caution if you have kidney problems, as your dose may need to be adjusted. It is given by IV infusion in a hospital or clinic setting, not as a pill at home.
typical_dosing: The usual adult dose is 2 grams given through an IV (directly into a vein) over 3 hours, every 8 hours for 7 to 14 days depending on the type of infection. The dose may be lower or given less often if you have kidney problems. This medication is always given by a healthcare professional in a medical setting.
